::: {.lead}
A player opens *Pocket Quest* on a phone. Music plays in another app, a chat
app waits for messages, and an update downloads. The phone has one screen,
a few CPU cores and a few gigabytes of RAM, but all these apps seem to run
at once. Who decides which app uses the CPU, and how much memory each one
gets? The **operating system** (OS). In lectures 3 to 8 you met the
hardware. In this lesson you meet the software that manages it: what the OS
does for a game, how it shares the CPU between **processes**, and how it
shares the RAM. Every section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary operating-system os-services process multitasking scheduler time-slice process-state foreground-app background-app memory-management virtual-memory task-manager >}}

## 9.1 What the OS does for a game

*Pocket Quest* wants to show a picture, read a tap, save the progress and
play a sound. It does not talk to the GPU, the touch screen, the storage or
the speaker by itself. It asks the operating system, and the OS does the job
(@fig-layers).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 9.1 — Operating system and its services"}
The **operating system** is the software that manages the hardware and gives
services to all other programs. Its main services are: running **processes**
on the CPU, sharing the **memory**, keeping **files** in storage, controlling
**devices** (screen, touch, sound, camera) and checking **permissions**.
:::

![The OS works between the apps and the hardware. Every app asks the OS for the CPU, memory, files and devices.](images/os-layers.png){#fig-layers width=96%}

Windows, macOS and Linux are operating systems for computers; Android and
iOS are operating systems for phones and tablets. Lecture 13 looks inside
Android and iOS.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.1 — The player taps the game icon"}
1. **Files:** the OS finds the game in storage and loads it into RAM
   (lecture 2).
2. **Processes:** the OS starts a new process for the game and gives it CPU
   time.
3. **Memory:** the OS gives the process its own part of the RAM.
4. **Devices:** the OS sends every tap to the game and shows its frames on
   the screen.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.2 — The game asks for the microphone"}
*Pocket Quest* has voice chat. The first time, the phone shows: "Allow
Pocket Quest to record audio?" This is the **permission** service. If the
player says no, the OS does not give the game the microphone, and voice chat
stays silent.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that the OS is only the home screen and the icons. The home screen
is only one part. Most of the OS works where the player cannot see it:
sharing the CPU, the RAM and the devices.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Name your two operating systems"}
On the lab computer, open Settings › System › About (Windows: Win + I). On
your phone, open Settings › About phone (iPhone: Settings › General ›
About).

1. Write the name and the version of each OS.
2. Write one service of the OS that you used today, and what it did.

*Your result:* two OS names with versions, and one service.
:::

## 9.2 Many apps, few cores: processes and the scheduler

The phone has 8 CPU cores, but more than 100 processes. A PC can have 200.
They cannot all run on a core at the same moment. The OS **switches** between
them very fast (@fig-slices).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 9.2 — Process, scheduler and time slice"}
A **process** is a running program with its own part of memory. The
**scheduler** of the OS decides which process runs on a core, for a short
**time slice** of a few milliseconds, and then switches to the next one.
This is **multitasking**. At each moment, a process is **running** (on a
core), **ready** (waiting for a core) or **waiting** (for a file, the
network or a tap).
:::

![One core shared by three processes in time slices of 4 ms. The switches are so fast that all apps seem to run at once.](images/time-slices.png){#fig-slices width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.3 — Three processes on one core"}
To keep the numbers simple, take one core and slices of 4 ms. The game,
the music app and a download are ready.

1. The scheduler gives each one 4 ms in turn: game, music, download, game, …
2. In every 12 ms, the game runs for 4 ms: one third of the time.
3. The player closes the download. Now the game runs 4 ms of every 8 ms:
   half of the time. The game gets faster.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.4 — Waiting for a file"}
The game loads the next level from storage. Until the data arrives, the game
process is **waiting**: the scheduler gives its slices to the music app.
When the file is loaded, the game is **ready** again. A slow drive makes the
game wait longer (lecture 3).
:::

The OS gives the **foreground app** (the one on the screen) more CPU time
than the **background apps**. A phone OS even pauses most background apps.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"Eight cores, so eight apps at most." A core runs one process at a time, but
the scheduler switches many times per second, so hundreds of processes share
the cores.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/scheduler-lab.html" poster="sims/scheduler-lab.png" title="Scheduler Lab: one core, many processes" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The processes of the lab computer"}
Open **Task Manager** (Ctrl + Shift + Esc) and choose the Processes tab
(press "More details" if you see only a short list).

1. How many apps and how many background processes are there?
2. Which three processes use the most memory?

*Your result:* two numbers and three process names with their memory.
:::

## 9.3 Sharing the RAM: memory management

The player leaves *Pocket Quest* to take a photo for a quest. When the player
comes back, the game starts again from the title screen. What happened? The
RAM was full, and the OS took memory back (@fig-ram).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 9.3 — Memory management"}
**Memory management** is the job of the OS that gives each process its own
part of the RAM, keeps these parts apart (one app cannot read another app's
memory) and takes the memory back when a process ends. When the RAM is full,
a **phone** OS closes background apps; a **computer** OS moves data that is
not used now to the drive, as **virtual memory** (Windows: the page file).
:::

![A 4 GB phone. The OS, the game and the camera need 4.2 GB, so the OS closes the background game.](images/ram-full.png){#fig-ram width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.5 — Pocket Quest and the camera"}
The phone has 4 GB of RAM. The OS uses 1.5 GB and Pocket Quest 1.8 GB.

1. In use: 1.5 + 1.8 = 3.3 GB. Free: 4 − 3.3 = 0.7 GB.
2. The player opens the camera, which needs 0.9 GB. 3.3 + 0.9 = 4.2 GB: more
   than 4 GB.
3. The game is now in the background, so the OS closes it and frees 1.8 GB.
   The camera on the screen keeps running.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.6 — The same on a PC"}
A PC has 8 GB of RAM. The OS uses 2 GB, a game 6 GB and a browser 3 GB:
11 GB.

1. Windows does not close the browser. It moves memory that is not used now
   to the page file on the drive.
2. The drive is much slower than RAM (lecture 3), so the PC slows down when
   the player switches between the apps.
:::

Because a phone OS may close a game in the background at any time, a good
mobile game **saves its state** when it goes to the background. Then it can
continue at the same place after a restart.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"The game crashed." When a mobile game starts again after the player used
other apps, it often did not crash: the OS closed it to free RAM. The fix is
to save the state, not to look for a bug in the game.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The memory of the lab computer"}
In **Task Manager**, open the Performance tab and choose Memory.

1. Write the total RAM, the RAM in use and the RAM available.
2. Open three browser tabs with videos. How much does "in use" grow?

*Your result:* three numbers before, and the new "in use" after.
:::

## Case study: Pocket Quest on a 4 GB phone

*Pocket Quest* is a made-up adventure game by the studio *Byte Bay*. It runs
on a phone with 4 GB of RAM. The OS takes 1.5 GB, and the game 1.8 GB. In
one quest, the player must take a photo with the camera (0.9 GB) and come
back. Later the game loads a bigger level of 2.3 GB while Chat (0.4 GB, used
1 minute ago) and Music (0.3 GB, used 20 minutes ago) wait in the
background. The team must know what the OS will do each time. The Game
challenge of the interactive lesson uses these numbers. In the mini-game
below you are the OS.

{{< sim file="sims/ram-rush.html" poster="sims/ram-rush.png" title="RAM Rush: you are the operating system of a phone" kind="game" height="640" >}}

## Further reading

Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, *Operating System Concepts*, 10th ed.,
Chapter 1 (what operating systems do), Chapter 3 (processes) and Chapter 9
(main memory). Tanenbaum and Austin, *Structured Computer Organization*,
6th ed., Chapter 6 (the operating system machine level).

## Exercises

1. Name four services of an operating system.
2. Name two operating systems for computers and two for phones.
3. A game wants to use the camera. Which service of the OS decides if it may?
4. What is a process? What does the scheduler do?
5. What are the three states of a process? Give a game example of each.
6. One core, slices of 4 ms. A game and three other processes are ready.
   How many ms of every 16 ms does the game run?
7. A phone has 6 GB of RAM. The OS uses 2 GB and a game 2.5 GB. How much is
   free?
8. On the phone of exercise 7, the player opens an app of 2 GB. What does
   the OS do?
9. What does Windows do when the RAM is full? Why does the PC get slower?
10. *Pocket Quest*: the game loads a level of 2.3 GB, with Chat (0.4 GB) and
    Music (0.3 GB) in the background. Which apps does the OS close, and why
    in this order?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. For example: running processes, sharing memory, keeping files, controlling devices, checking permissions.
2. Computers: Windows, macOS, Linux. Phones: Android, iOS.
3. The permission service: the player allows or refuses the camera.
4. A running program with its own memory. The scheduler decides which process runs on a core, and for how long.
5. Running (the game computes a frame), ready (the game waits for a core), waiting (the game waits for a file to load).
6. 4 ms of every 16 ms (one quarter).
7. 6 − 2 − 2.5 = 1.5 GB.
8. 4.5 + 2 = 6.5 GB is more than 6 GB: the OS closes the game if it is in the background.
9. It moves memory that is not used now to the page file on the drive; the drive is much slower than RAM.
10. 1.5 + 2.3 + 0.4 + 0.3 = 4.5 GB. It closes Music first (used longest ago), then Chat, because 4.2 GB is still too much.
:::
